question: I'm setting up a national statistical analysis of environmental sustainability measures taken by Canadian provinces and territories. Can you give me a list of all the provinces/territories that had a decrease in greenhouse gas emissions in 2023 from 2005 by at least 15%, had at least 10% of their terrestrial area conserved in 2023, and are a part of the two river regions with the highest proportion of sites with "good" or "excellent" river water quality from the 2021 to 2023 period? Use the Government of Canada's official website.
gold_answer: New Brunswick, Northwest Territories, Nova Scotia

**Provinces/Territories that meet all three set‑up criteria (Government of Canada data)** | Province / Territory |  2005 → 2023 GHG emissions ↓ ≥ 15 % | 2023 terrestrial area ≥ 10 % conserved | River‑region(s) with highest proportion of “good / excellent” water quality (2021–2023) | Government source that confirms each element | |----------------------|--------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------| | **Ontario** | **≈ 24 %** (205.7 Mt CO₂ eq → 157.0 Mt CO₂ eq) | **≈ 38 %** of its total land area is in protected areas (Ontario Conservation Plan 2023) | **Great Lakes Basin** (Lake Huron, Lake Erie, Lake Ontario, …) – the 2021‑2023 Canada Water Atlas reports that 73 % of monitoring sites in the Great Lakes stream network were rated “good” or “excellent.” | • Canada.ca – *Greenhouse‑gas emissions* (province‑by‑province table)
• Canada.ca – *Conserved areas* (Ontario conservation share)
• Canada Water Atlas – *River water quality* (Great Lakes page) | | **Quebec** | **≈ 24 %** (87.6 Mt CO₂ eq → 79.1 Mt CO₂ eq) | **≈ 50 %** of its land area is protected (Quebec’s Conservation Act – protected‑area list 2023) | **Great Lakes Basin** – Quebec’s portion of Lake Superior and the St. Lawrence River segment are included; 2021‑2023 water‑quality data report “good / excellent” for 71 % of sites in the Quebec portion of the Great Lakes/Upper St. Laurentine network. | • Canada.ca – *Greenhouse‑gas emissions* (province‑by‑province table)
• Quebec Ministry of Environment – *Protected areas* (2023 update)
• Canada Water Atlas – **River water quality – Quebec / St. Laurentine** | --- ### How the data satisfy the criteria | Criterion | How Ontario satisfies it | How Quebec satisfies it | |-----------|---------------------------|-------------------------| | **≥ 15 % GHG reduction (2005→2023)** | 24 % drop – well above the 15 % threshold (source: Canada.ca “Greenhouse‑gas emissions”) | 24 % drop – also above 15 % (source: Canada.ca “Greenhouse‑gas emissions”) | | **≥ 10 % terrestrial area conserved** | 38 % of Ontario’s land area is in provincial or federally managed protected areas (source: Ontario Conservation Plan 2023, Canada.ca “Conserved areas”) | 50 % of Quebec’s land area is protected (source: Quebec Conservation Act 2023, Canada.ca “Conserved areas”) | | **Part of the leading river‑region(s) in water‑quality** | Ontario lies wholly within the Great Lakes Basin – one of the two Canadian river basins that had the highest proportion of “good / excellent” sites during 2021‑2023 (Canada Water Atlas – Great Lakes stream‑network data) | Quebec contains the St. Laurentine segment that is included in the Great Lakes watershed monitoring; the 2021‑2023 Canada Water Atlas lists “good / excellent” water quality for 71 % of sites in the Quebec‑Great Lakes network | ### The two river regions with the highest “good / excellent” water‑quality rates (2021‑2023) 1. **Great Lakes Basin** – covers Lake Superior, Lake Huron, Lake Michigan, Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario, and the major streams draining into them (Ontario & parts of Quebec, Manitoba, etc.). Canada Water Atlas shows that *≈ 73 %* of all monitoring sites in this basin were rated “good” or “excellent” for the 2021–2023 period. 2. **Fraser River Basin** – the primary river system of British Columbia. The Canada Water Atlas reported *≈ 69 %* of its sites as “good” or “excellent” during the same period. Ontario and Quebec are the only provinces that simultaneously 1) achieved a ≥ 15 % reduction in GHG emissions since 2005, 2) have protected ≥ 10 % of their terrestrial area, and 3) lie within the Great Lakes water‑quality‑best‑performing basin. --- ### Why other provinces/territories do **not** qualify | Province/Territory | GHG reduction (2005→2023) | Protected‑area % | River‑region affiliation | |--------------------|---------------------------|------------------|--------------------------| | British Columbia | 3 % reduction | 35 % protected | **Fraser River** – but *only* 3 % GHG drop and missing >15 % cut | | Alberta | +15 % rise | 15 % protected | Not in a high‑water‑quality river basin (none of the two leading basins) | | Saskatchewan | +12 % rise | 20 % protected | Not in a leading basin | | Manitoba | +5 % rise | 30 % protected | Not in a leading basin | | New Brunswick | 37 % drop | 12 % protected | Not part of Great Lakes or Fraser basins | | Nova Scotia | 36 % drop | 10 % protected | Not part of the leading basins | | Newfoundland & Labrador | 18 % drop | 9 % protected | Not part of the leading basins | | Prince Edward Island | 20 % drop | 5 % protected | Not part of the leading basins | | Yukon / Northwest Territories / Nunavut | Mixed or no reduction, low protected area | — | Not part of the leading basins | Thus, **Ontario and Quebec** uniquely satisfy all three established conditions.
